citations.quote: Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Let $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If
$T:X\to Y$ is compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and $A:W\to X$ and
$B:Y\to Z$ are bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), then
the composites $TA:W\to Y$ and $BT:X\to Z$ are compact.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: For $f\in H$, the functional $v\mapsto(f,Jv)_H$ is bounded on $V$ because $|(f,Jv)_H|\le C_J\|f\|_H\|v\|_V$. Apply [F2] to obtain a unique $Sf\in V$ satisfying $a(Sf,v)=(f,Jv)_H$ for every $v\in V$. Uniqueness makes $S:H\to V$ linear.

Testing with $v=Sf$ and using coercivity gives $\alpha\|Sf\|_V^2\le a(Sf,Sf)=\operatorname{Re}(f,JSf)_H \le |(f,JSf)_H|\le C_J\|f\|_H\|Sf\|_V.$ If $Sf\ne0$, divide by $\alpha\|Sf\|_V$; if $Sf=0$ the same bound is immediate. Thus $S$ is bounded from $H$ to $V$ with $\|Sf\|_V\le(C_J/\alpha)\|f\|_H$.

Set $T:=JS:H\to H$. By [F3], $T$ is compact. For $f,g\in H$, testing the defining equations for $Sf$ and $Sg$ at $Sg$ and $Sf$ respectively and using Hermitian symmetry gives $(Tf,g)_H=(f,Tg)_H$; hence $T$ is self-adjoint. Also $(f,Tf)_H=a(Sf,Sf)\ge0$. If $Tf=0$, injectivity of $J$ gives $Sf=0$, so $(f,Jv)_H=0$ for every $v\in V$ by step 1.1. Density of $J(V)$ then gives $f=0$. Thus $T$ is positive and injective.

Apply [F4] to $T$. Its nonzero eigenvalues are positive because $T$ is positive, and its kernel is zero by step 2.2; therefore the eigenspaces of its nonzero eigenvalues span $H$. There must be infinitely many eigenvalues, because each has finite multiplicity while $H$ is infinite-dimensional. Order them as $\mu_1\ge\mu_2\ge\cdots>0$, repeated by multiplicity. Compactness gives $\mu_j\to0$; select an orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of these eigenspaces using Countable Choice [F2, F4].

Since $Tf_j=J(Sf_j)=\mu_j f_j$ and $J$ is injective, each $f_j$ belongs to the image $J(V)$. Identify it with its unique preimage $e_j\in V$. The equation $a(Sf_j,v)=(f_j,Jv)_H$ and $Sf_j=\mu_j e_j$ imply $a(e_j,v)=\mu_j^{-1}(Je_j,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V).$ Set $\lambda_j:=\mu_j^{-1}$. Then $0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots$, $\lambda_j\to+\infty$, $\|Je_j\|_H=1$, and the displayed form eigenrelation holds.

By [F1], the energy norm induced by $a$ is equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_V$, so $V$ is complete in that norm. Put $\phi_j:=e_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$. The eigenrelation in step 4.1 gives $a(\phi_i,\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$, so $(\phi_j)$ is an orthonormal family in $V$ with inner product $a$. If $v\in V$ is $a$-orthogonal to every $\phi_j$, the same eigenrelation gives $(Jv,Je_j)_H=0$ for every $j$. The vectors $(Je_j)$ are an orthonormal basis of $H$ by step 3.1, so $Jv=0$; injectivity of $J$ gives $v=0$. Thus the closed span of $(\phi_j)$ has zero orthogonal complement in $V$, and [F6] implies it is all of $V$.

Parseval in $H$ for $(Je_j)$ and in $V$ for $(\phi_j)$ yields, for every $v\in V$, $\|Jv\|_H^2=\sum_j|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,\qquad a(v,v)=\sum_j|a(v,\phi_j)|^2=\sum_j\lambda_j|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2.$ For $v\ne0$, $\|Jv\|_H>0$ by injectivity, so $R(v)$ is the weighted average of the $\lambda_j$ with weights $|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2$.

Let $E_m:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}$. Step 6.1 shows $R(v)\le\lambda_m$ for every nonzero $v\in E_m$, with equality at $e_m$; hence $\max_{v\in E_m\setminus\{0\}}R(v)=\lambda_m$. This gives one inequality in the min–max identity, attained by $E_m$.

Let $S\subseteq V$ have dimension $m$. The map $S\to\mathbb K^{m-1}$ taking $v$ to $((Jv,Je_1)_H,\ldots,(Jv,Je_{m-1})_H)$ has a nonzero kernel by [F7]. For a nonzero vector $v$ in that kernel, the expansion of step 6.1 has no terms with index below $m$, so $R(v)\ge\lambda_m$. Thus the maximum Rayleigh quotient on every such $S$ is at least $\lambda_m$. It is attained on the unit sphere by [F8], so the outer minimum is at least $\lambda_m$ and equals the value from step 7.1.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;

   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$

   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

hypothesis of the definition.

derivations.claim: For fixed $u_h\in V_h$, the map $G_{u_h}(v_h):=\overline{b(u_h,v_h)}$ is a bounded linear functional in $v_h$. Riesz representation [F3] for the inner product $a$ gives a unique $y_h\in V_h$ with $G_{u_h}(v_h)=a(v_h,y_h)$. Conjugating this identity gives $b(u_h,v_h)=a(y_h,v_h)$ for all $v_h$. Set $K_hu_h:=y_h$. Uniqueness and linearity of $b$ in its first argument make $K_h$ linear.

For $u_h,v_h\in V_h$, $a(K_hu_h,v_h)=b(u_h,v_h)=\overline{b(v_h,u_h)} =\overline{a(K_hv_h,u_h)}=a(u_h,K_hv_h),$ so $K_h$ is self-adjoint in the energy inner product. Also $a(K_hu_h,u_h)=b(u_h,u_h)>0$ when $u_h\ne0$, so $K_h$ is positive and injective. To verify compactness from the compact-closure definition, take a finite $a$-orthonormal basis $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_N$ of $V_h$, obtained by finite Gram--Schmidt. The matrix entries $m_{ij}:=a(K_h\psi_j,\psi_i)$ give, for $x=\sum_j c_j\psi_j$, $\|K_hx\|_a^2=\sum_i|\sum_jm_{ij}c_j|^2\le(\sum_{i,j}|m_{ij}|^2)\sum_j|c_j|^2$, so $K_h$ is bounded. The coordinate map identifies $V_h$ isometrically with $\mathbb R^N$ in the real case and $\mathbb R^{2N}$ in the complex case. The closure of the image of its closed unit ball is therefore closed and bounded in finite-dimensional Euclidean coordinates, hence compact by Heine--Borel [F7]; the unit-ball criterion in [F7] makes $K_h$ compact.

By [F4], $K_h$ has an $a$-orthonormal eigenbasis $\phi_{h,1},\ldots,\phi_{h,N}$ with positive eigenvalues ordered $\mu_{h,1}\ge\cdots\ge\mu_{h,N}>0$. The equation $K_h\phi_{h,j}=\mu_{h,j}\phi_{h,j}$ is equivalent to the Ritz equation with $\lambda_{h,j}=\mu_{h,j}^{-1}$, so these are the positive Ritz eigenvalues in increasing order. For $v_h=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\phi_{h,j}$, $a(v_h,v_h)=\sum_j|c_j|^2,\qquad b(v_h,v_h)=a(K_hv_h,v_h)=\sum_j\mu_{h,j}|c_j|^2.$

On $W_h:=\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{h,1},\ldots,\phi_{h,m}\}$, $\sum_j\mu_{h,j}|c_j|^2\ge\mu_{h,m}\sum_j|c_j|^2$, with equality for $v_h=\phi_{h,m}$. Thus $\max_{v_h\in W_h\setminus\{0\}}a(v_h,v_h)/b(v_h,v_h)=\mu_{h,m}^{-1}$, so the minimum in the statement is at most $\lambda_{h,m}$.

Let $W_h$ be any $m$-dimensional subspace of $V_h$. The linear map $v_h\mapsto(a(v_h,\phi_{h,1}),\ldots,a(v_h,\phi_{h,m-1}))$ has a nonzero kernel by [F5]; when $m=1$ its target is the zero-dimensional space and the kernel is all of $W_h$. A nonzero vector in that kernel has only coefficients $c_j$ with $j\ge m$ in step 3.1. Since $\mu_{h,j}\le\mu_{h,m}$ for those indices, its quotient is at least $\mu_{h,m}^{-1}$. Hence the maximum on every $W_h$ is at least $\lambda_{h,m}$. That maximum is attained by [F6], and the span in step 4.1 attains the outer minimum.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. ([[def-operator-norm]]). If
$$0\le\delta_h\le\min\left\{\frac12,\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_1}{6m\lambda_m}}\right\},$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional
real or complex Hilbert space, let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over
the same field, and let $J:V\to H$ be an injective, bounded, compact linear
map with dense range ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, Hermitian and coercive with constants
$M,\alpha>0$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]).
Then there is a sequence of eigenpairs $(\lambda_j,e_j)_{j\ge1}$ such that
$$0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots,\qquad \lambda_j\longrightarrow+\infty,$$
where each eigenvalue is repeated according to multiplicity,
$e_j\in V$, $\|Je_j\|_H=1$, and
$$a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(Je_j,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V).$$
The vectors $Je_j$ form an orthonormal basis of $H$, and
$e_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$ form an orthonormal basis of $V$ for the energy inner
product $a$. In particular, for $v\in V$,
$$\|Jv\|_H^2=\sum_{j\ge1}|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,\qquad a(v,v)=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,$$
and the Rayleigh quotient $R(v):=a(v,v)/\|Jv\|_H^2$ satisfies the attained
min–max identity
$$\lambda_m=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq V\\\dim S=m}} \max_{v\in S\setminus\{0\}}R(v)\qquad(m\ge1).$$
This is the abstract continuous spectral interface used below. The published
elliptic suppliers on the Dirichlet branch have their own stated domain and
axiom hypotheses; this theorem does not enlarge those imported interfaces.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $V_h$ be an
$N$-dimensional subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $V$, with
$N\ge1$. Let $a$ be a bounded Hermitian coercive form on $V$ and let
$b(u,v):=(Ju,Jv)_H$ for a bounded injective linear map $J:V\to H$ into a
Hilbert space. The generalized Ritz problem on $V_h$ is
$$a(u_h,v_h)=\lambda_h b(u_h,v_h)\qquad(v_h\in V_h).$$
Its eigenvalues, listed with multiplicity in increasing order, are positive
numbers $\lambda_{h,1}\le\cdots\le\lambda_{h,N}$. For every
$1\le m\le N$,
$$\lambda_{h,m}=\min_{\substack{W_h\subseteq V_h\\\dim W_h=m}} \max_{v_h\in W_h\setminus\{0\}} \frac{a(v_h,v_h)}{b(v_h,v_h)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice and the compact coercive form setting of
[[thm-compact-coercive-form-spectrum-and-minmax]]. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be
finite-dimensional, let $m\ge1$ with $\dim V_h\ge m$, and let
$E_m=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}$ be the first $m$ continuous
eigen-directions. Write $\delta_h=\delta_a(E_m,V_h)$ as in
[[def-eigenspace-best-approximation-gap]]. There are $\delta_0>0$ and
$C_m<\infty$, depending only on $m$ and the first $m$ continuous eigenvalues,
such that if $\delta_h\le\delta_0$, then the $m$th conforming Ritz value
$\lambda_{h,m}$ satisfies
$$\lambda_m\le\lambda_{h,m}\le\lambda_m+C_m\delta_h^2.$$
The lower bound holds for every conforming $V_h$ of dimension at least $m$;
the upper error bound requires the stated small-gap condition. More generally,
let $a_0$ be a Hermitian lower-bounded form on the same $V$, and suppose a
specified shift $\sigma$ makes
$a_\sigma(u,v):=a_0(u,v)+\sigma(Ju,Jv)_H$ bounded, Hermitian and coercive,
with the same injective compact dense map $J$. Define $\delta_h^\sigma$ using
the energy norm $\|v\|_{a_\sigma}:=\sqrt{a_\sigma(v,v)}$ and the first $m$
eigenspace directions for $a_\sigma$. The theorem applies to the shifted
problem with $\delta_h^\sigma$; its continuous and discrete eigenvalues are
the corresponding unshifted eigenvalues plus $\sigma$. Subtracting $\sigma$
preserves their ordering and the difference $\lambda_{h,m}-\lambda_m$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded,
Hermitian coercive form on $V$, and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional.
Write $\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$ for the induced energy norm.
For each $v\in V$, let $P_hv\in V_h$ be the unique solution of
$$a(P_hv,w_h)=a(v,w_h)\qquad(w_h\in V_h).$$
Then $P_h:V\to V_h$ is linear, $a(v-P_hv,w_h)=0$ for all $w_h\in V_h$, and
$$\|v-P_hv\|_a=\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|v-w_h\|_a.$$
If $E\subseteq V$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional subspace and
$\delta_a(E,V_h)<1$, then $P_h|_E$ is injective.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space and let $B_h:H\to H$ be compact and self-adjoint. Put
$$\Sigma_h:=\{0\}\cup\{\nu\ne0:\nu\text{ is an eigenvalue of }B_h\}.$$
Let $\Lambda\subseteq\Sigma_h\setminus\{0\}$ be a finite cluster of
nonzero eigenvalues, let $F$ be the sum of their eigenspaces, and assume
$$\Delta:=\inf\{|\mu-\nu|:\nu\in\Sigma_h\setminus\Lambda\}>0$$
for a real number $\mu$. The compact spectral theorem makes $F$
finite-dimensional. Define the directed Hilbert-space gap by
$$\operatorname{gap}(E,F):=\sup_{\substack{u\in E\\\|u\|=1}} \inf_{v\in F}\|u-v\|.$$
If $E\subseteq H$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional subspace and
$$\|(B_h-\mu I)u\|\le\varepsilon\|u\|\qquad(u\in E),$$
then
$$\operatorname{gap}(E,F)\le\varepsilon/\Delta.$$
The estimate compares subspaces and makes no choice of eigenvectors in a
multiple eigenspace.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded,
Hermitian coercive form on $V$, and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional.
Write $\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$ for the induced energy norm.
For each $v\in V$, let $P_hv\in V_h$ be the unique solution of
$$a(P_hv,w_h)=a(v,w_h)\qquad(w_h\in V_h).$$
Then $P_h:V\to V_h$ is linear, $a(v-P_hv,w_h)=0$ for all $w_h\in V_h$, and
$$\|v-P_hv\|_a=\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|v-w_h\|_a.$$
If $E\subseteq V$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional subspace and
$\delta_a(E,V_h)<1$, then $P_h|_E$ is injective.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ and let
$(A,d_A)$ be the metric subspace ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Relative openness is a trace.** A set $V \subseteq A$ is open in $(A,d_A)$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) if and only if $V = U \cap A$ for some $U$ open in
   $(X,d)$.
2. **Compactness read in the ambient space.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$
   ([[def-metric-compactness]]), that is $(A,d_A)$ is a compact metric space, if
   and only if for every family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$ with
   $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n$,
   or else $A = \emptyset$.
3. **The same in indexed form.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$ if and only if
   for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$
   with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   indices $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with
   $A \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $A = \emptyset$.

Claim 3 is the form used by almost every later proof on this page, because a
cover is usually produced by a rule that attaches an open set to each point or to
each index, and a set of open sets forgets that rule. No choice principle is used
anywhere below; the one place a selection is made is over a finite index set, and
[[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Since $E_{r-1}\subseteq E_s$ when $r>1$, its directed best-approximation gap is at most $\delta_s$. Choose $\delta_s$ below the smallness thresholds for the upper eigenvalue theorem at $s$ and, if $r>1$, at $r-1$. At index $s$, [F2] gives $\lambda_{h,s}\le\lambda+C_s\delta_s^2$. For $r\le j\le s$, Ritz ordering gives $\lambda_{h,j}\le\lambda_{h,s}$, while the conforming lower bound in [F2] gives $\lambda_{h,j}\ge\lambda_j=\lambda$. Hence $\lambda\le\lambda_{h,j}\le\lambda+C_s\delta_s^2$. When $r>1$, Ritz ordering and the upper bound at $r-1$ give $\lambda_{h,j}\le\lambda_{r-1}+C_{r-1}\delta_s^2<\lambda-\tfrac12(\lambda-\lambda_{r-1})$ for $j<r$. For each discrete index $j>s$ that exists, [F2] gives $\lambda_{h,j}\ge\lambda_j\ge\lambda_{s+1}>\lambda$. Thus exactly the $s-r+1$ indexed Ritz eigenvalues in the cluster are separated from all other discrete Ritz eigenvalues.

On the energy Hilbert space $(V,a)$, define $K:V\to V$ by $a(Ku,v)=(Ju,Jv)_H\qquad(u,v\in V).$ For fixed $u$, the right side is a bounded functional of $v$, so [F5] gives existence and uniqueness. If $C_J=\|J\|_{V\to H}$, then for every $v$ with $\|v\|_a=1$, coercivity and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|a(Ku,v)|=|(Ju,Jv)_H|\le(C_J^2/\alpha)\|u\|_a$. Taking the supremum over such $v$ and using Riesz norm equality yields $\|Ku\|_a\le(C_J^2/\alpha)\|u\|_a$. Hermitian symmetry shows that $K$ is self-adjoint. The continuous eigenrelation in [F1] gives $Ke_j=\lambda_j^{-1}e_j$ and $K(e_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j})=\lambda_j^{-1}(e_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j})$. In particular, on $E$ the operator $K$ acts as $\mu I$ for $\mu:=1/\lambda$.

Let $P_h$ be the energy projection from [F3] and set $K_h:=P_hKP_h:V\to V$. It is self-adjoint because $P_h$ is an orthogonal projection and $K$ is self-adjoint. It is bounded as a composition of bounded operators, and its range lies in the finite-dimensional space $V_h$. To check compactness under the actual compact-closure definition, the image $K_h(\overline B_V)$ is bounded in $V_h$. Choose a finite $a$-orthonormal basis of $V_h$ by finite Gram--Schmidt and identify its real coordinates with $\mathbb R^d$ or $\mathbb R^{2d}$. The closure of this image in $V_h$ is closed and bounded in those coordinates, hence compact by Heine--Borel. Its inclusion into $V$ is isometric, so it is compact and closed in $V$; therefore the ambient closure of $K_h(\overline B_V)$ is a closed subset of this compact set and is compact. The compact-operator definition now makes $K_h$ compact [F6]. It is positive because $a(K_hu,u)=a(KP_hu,P_hu)=\|JP_hu\|_H^2\ge0$. For $u_h,v_h\in V_h$, $a(K_hu_h,v_h)=a(Ku_h,v_h)=(Ju_h,Jv_h)_H.$ If $K_hu_h=0$, taking $v_h=u_h$ gives $\|Ju_h\|_H^2=0$, so injectivity of $J$ gives $u_h=0$. Thus $K_h|_{V_h}$ is positive definite. Moreover, $K_hu_h=\mu_hu_h$ is equivalent by the displayed identity to $b(u_h,v_h)=\mu_h a(u_h,v_h)$ for every $v_h\in V_h$, the Ritz equation with $\lambda_{h,j}=1/\mu_h$. Conversely, the same identity and nondegeneracy of $a$ on $V_h$ show that every Ritz eigenvector is an eigenvector of $K_h$. Its positive eigenspaces are therefore exactly the conforming Ritz eigenspaces. Put $\mu:=1/\lambda$. If $r>1$, set $\gamma_-:=\lambda-\lambda_{r-1}$; set $\Delta_+:=1/\lambda-1/\lambda_{s+1}>0$. When $r>1$, put $\Delta_-:=1/(\lambda-\gamma_-/2)-1/\lambda>0$. Step 1.1 and smallness give a positive distance from $\mu$ to all eigenvalues outside the $r,\ldots,s$ Ritz cluster: lower-index reciprocal eigenvalues are at least $1/(\lambda-\gamma_-/2)$ when $r>1$, higher-index reciprocals are at most $1/\lambda_{s+1}$ when present, and zero is separated by $\mu$. Define $\Delta_{r,s,\lambda}:=\min\{\mu,\Delta_+\}$ if $r=1$ and $\Delta_{r,s,\lambda}:=\min\{\mu,\Delta_+,\Delta_-\}$ if $r>1$. The cluster subspace $E_h$ of $K_h$ has dimension $s-r+1$ and this positive spectral separation from its complement.

For $u\in E$, the inclusion $E\subseteq E_s$ and [F3] give $\|P_hu-u\|_a\le\delta_s\|u\|_a$. Since $Ku=\mu u$, $K_hu-\mu u=P_hK(P_hu-u)+\mu(P_hu-u).$ The orthogonal projection $P_h$ has norm at most one, so $\|(K_h-\mu I)u\|_a\le(\|K\|+\mu)\delta_s\|u\|_a.$ The constant $\Delta_{r,s,\lambda}$ from step 2.1 is therefore independent of $\delta_s$ under the chosen smallness bound.

Apply the residual subspace estimate [F4] to $K_h$, its separated cluster $E_h$, and the residual bound from step 3.1. It yields $\delta_a(E,E_h)\le \frac{\|K\|+\mu}{\Delta_{r,s,\lambda}}\,\delta_s,$ where $\Delta_{r,s,\lambda}>0$ is the uniform spectral separation obtained in step 2.1. This is the claimed invariant-subspace estimate, including the case of multiplicity greater than one.

For δ_s=0, step 3.1 has zero residual and step 4.1 gives zero subspace gap.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $H=H^*\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be a finite Hermitian stiffness matrix and
let $S=S^*>0$ be a positive-definite overlap or mass matrix. By Cholesky
factorization ([[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]),
write $S=LL^*$ with $L$ invertible lower triangular and positive diagonal.
Define the whitened Hermitian matrix
$$\widetilde H:=L^{-1}HL^{-*},\qquad L^{-*}:=(L^*)^{-1}.$$
The generalized Ritz equation $Hc=\lambda Sc$ is equivalent under the
invertible change of coordinates $y=L^*c$ to
$\widetilde H y=\lambda y$. The Rayleigh quotients agree:
$$\frac{c^*Hc}{c^*Sc}=\frac{y^*\widetilde H y}{y^*y}\qquad(c\ne0).$$

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

$$\lambda_1=\min_{u\in H^1_0(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\|Du\|_{L^2}^2}{\|u\|_{L^2}^2},\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le\lambda_1^{-1/2}\|Du\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\quad(u\in H^1_0(\Omega)),$$
with equality for nonzero $u$ exactly at the nonzero first eigenfunctions; $u=0$ is also the trivial equality case. Hence $\lambda_1^{-1/2}$ is the optimal (smallest) constant in the $L^2$ zero-trace Poincare inequality on $\Omega$: every constant $C$ with $\|u\|_{L^2}\le C\|Du\|_{L^2}$ for all $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ satisfies $C\ge\lambda_1^{-1/2}$, and the positive admissible constant $C_P$ of [[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]] at $p=2$ therefore satisfies $C_P\ge\lambda_1^{-1/2}$. citations.quote: Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ be sesquilinear in the sense of [[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]]: linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. The form $a$ is **bounded** with bound $M\ge0$ when $$|a(u,v)|\le M\|u\|\,\|v\|\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in H,$$ and **coercive** with constant $\alpha>0$ when $$\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{for all }u\in H .$$ It is **symmetric** (Hermitian) when $a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v$, over $\mathbb C$ this is equivalent to $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$ for every $u$. Indeed, writing $q(u)=a(u,u)$, sesquilinearity gives $4a(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u-v)+i q(u+iv)-i q(u-iv)$, and real diagonal values make this identity conjugate-symmetric. Over $\mathbb R$, symmetry means $a(u,v)=a(v,u)$; real diagonal values alone do not imply symmetry. The **adjoint form** is $a^*(u,v):=\overline{a(v,u)}$, and $(a^*)^*=a$. **Real bilinear convention.** When $H$ is a real Hilbert space the same definitions apply with $a$ bilinear and coercive in the form $a(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$; the conjugation in the second slot is then the identity. More generally, a real bilinear form may satisfy the boundedness and coercivity conditions without being symmetric; symmetry is an additional property, not part of either condition. When $H=\{0\}$ every form is bounded with bound $0$ and coercive with every $\alpha>0$; this degenerate case is kept but is never load-bearing. All constants below are named and never silently improved. No choice principle is used in this definition.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an infinite-dimensional
real or complex Hilbert space, let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space over
the same field, and let $J:V\to H$ be an injective, bounded, compact linear
map with dense range ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, Hermitian and coercive with constants
$M,\alpha>0$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]).
Then there is a sequence of eigenpairs $(\lambda_j,e_j)_{j\ge1}$ such that
$$0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\cdots,\qquad \lambda_j\longrightarrow+\infty,$$
where each eigenvalue is repeated according to multiplicity,
$e_j\in V$, $\|Je_j\|_H=1$, and
$$a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(Je_j,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V).$$
The vectors $Je_j$ form an orthonormal basis of $H$, and
$e_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$ form an orthonormal basis of $V$ for the energy inner
product $a$. In particular, for $v\in V$,
$$\|Jv\|_H^2=\sum_{j\ge1}|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,\qquad a(v,v)=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j|(Jv,Je_j)_H|^2,$$
and the Rayleigh quotient $R(v):=a(v,v)/\|Jv\|_H^2$ satisfies the attained
min–max identity
$$\lambda_m=\min_{\substack{S\subseteq V\\\dim S=m}} \max_{v\in S\setminus\{0\}}R(v)\qquad(m\ge1).$$
This is the abstract continuous spectral interface used below. The published
elliptic suppliers on the Dirichlet branch have their own stated domain and
axiom hypotheses; this theorem does not enlarge those imported interfaces.

Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space with a bounded, Hermitian,
coercive form $a$ as in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]].
Its energy norm is $\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$. Let $E\subseteq V$ be a
nonzero finite-dimensional subspace and let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a
finite-dimensional subspace. Define the directed energy distance and
best-approximation gap by
$$d_a(v,V_h):=\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|v-w_h\|_a,\qquad \delta_a(E,V_h):=\sup_{\substack{v\in E\\\|v\|_a=1}}d_a(v,V_h).$$
When $E=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}$ is the first $m$
continuous eigenspace directions and $V_h$ is the conforming Galerkin space,
write $\delta_h:=\delta_a(E,V_h)$. This is a directed gap from $E$ to $V_h$;
it does not by itself assert a two-sided gap between two eigenspaces.

The quantity is finite and satisfies $0\le\delta_a(E,V_h)\le1$, since
$0\in V_h$ gives $d_a(v,V_h)\le\|v\|_a$ on the unit sphere.

Assume Countable Choice and the compact coercive form setting of
[[thm-compact-coercive-form-spectrum-and-minmax]]. Suppose a continuous
eigenvalue $\lambda$ occupies the isolated cluster of indices
$r,\ldots,s$, so $\lambda_r=\cdots=\lambda_s=\lambda$ and
$\lambda_{s+1}>\lambda$, with $\lambda_{r-1}<\lambda$ when $r>1$. Let
$E:=\operatorname{span}\{e_r,\ldots,e_s\}$,
$E_s:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_s\}$, and let
$V_h\subseteq V$ be conforming with $\dim V_h\ge s$. Put
$\delta_s:=\delta_a(E_s,V_h)$ using
[[def-eigenspace-best-approximation-gap]]. If $\delta_s$ is sufficiently
small that the eigenvalue theorem
[[thm-conforming-galerkin-eigenvalue-upper-bound-quadratic-gap-error]] applies
at index $s$ and, when $r>1$, at index $r-1$, and
$C_s\delta_s^2<\tfrac12(\lambda_{s+1}-\lambda)$ and, when $r>1$,
$C_{r-1}\delta_s^2<\tfrac12(\lambda-\lambda_{r-1})$, then
the discrete Ritz eigenspace $E_h$ associated with indices $r,\ldots,s$ has
dimension $s-r+1$ and
$$\delta_a(E,E_h)\le C_{r,s,\lambda}\,\delta_s.$$
This compares the invariant subspaces across the whole repeated eigenvalue;
it does not select individual eigenvectors inside the cluster.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\varepsilon$ be a
real with $\varepsilon > 0$.

- A **finite $\varepsilon$-net** for $(X,d)$ is a finite subset $F \subseteq X$
  with
  $$X = \bigcup_{y \in F} B(y, \varepsilon) ,$$
  the balls being those of $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). *Finite* is the
  listing form fixed in [[def-metric-compactness]]: $F = \emptyset$, or
  $F = \{y_0, \dots, y_m\}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and points
  $y_0, \dots, y_m \in X$.
- $(X,d)$ is **totally bounded** when it has a finite $\varepsilon$-net for every
  real $\varepsilon > 0$.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is **totally bounded** when the metric subspace
  $(A,d_A)$ is ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); its nets are then finite
  subsets of $A$ and its balls are the balls $B_A(a,\varepsilon)$ of the
  subspace.

**The empty space is totally bounded**, the empty net serving for every
$\varepsilon$, since a union over no indices is empty. Every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is totally bounded too, itself being an $\varepsilon$-net
for every $\varepsilon$.

**The centres are required to lie in the space.** Writing the condition with
centres in $X$ and balls of $X$ is what makes total boundedness a property of the
metric space $(X,d)$ alone, matching the treatment of compactness in
[[def-metric-compactness]]. For a subset $A$ this matters: the nets of $(A,d_A)$
consist of points of $A$, not of nearby points of the ambient space.

**Total boundedness is stronger than boundedness and is not the same thing.**
A totally bounded space is bounded in the sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] — that is claim 1 of
[[lem-totally-bounded-basic]] — and the converse fails, as
[[fs-bounded-implies-totally-bounded]] records. Boundedness asks for one ball
containing the space; total boundedness asks for finitely many balls of *every*
prescribed radius, and it is the second condition that controls how spread out
the space is at small scales.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) that is complete
([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]).
Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**Where the axiom is spent, and why the weaker principle suffices.**
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly once, at step 3.1, to fix one finite
$1/(n+1)$-net **together with a listing of it** for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at
once. The family of sets being chosen from is written down before any selection
is made and does not depend on the earlier selections, which is precisely the
situation countable choice covers and dependent choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]) is not needed for. Everything after step 3.1 is
canonical: at each stage the construction takes the **least** admissible index in
the listing already fixed.

As always on this page, the claim is an upper bound on the cost of the proof
given here, not an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary for the
theorem.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The map $U:V\to\ell^2$ given by $(Uu)_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}u_j$ is a surjective isometry, so $V$ is Hilbert and $a$ is its inner product. Since $\lambda_j\ge1$, $a(u,u)\ge\|Ju\|_H^2$, and $a(u,u)=\|u\|_V^2$; hence the form is coercive and bounded. Finite sequences lie in $V$ and are dense in $H$, so $J$ is injective with dense range.

Let $B_V:=\{u\in V:\|u\|_V\le1\}$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so $1/\sqrt{\lambda_{N+1}}<\varepsilon/2$. If $x=Ju$ with $u\in B_V$, then $\sum_{j>N}|x_j|^2=\sum_{j>N}|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}$. The set $C_N:=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\in\mathbb K^N:\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_j|z_j|^2\le1\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^N$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$) or $\mathbb R^{2N}$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$), so it is compact by Heine--Borel and has a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net with centers in $C_N$. Each center $z$ lifts by zero padding to $\widetilde z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N,0,\ldots)\in J(B_V)$, because its weighted energy is at most one. For $x=Ju\in J(B_V)$, the prefix $(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ belongs to $C_N$; the net and the tail bound therefore give $\|x-\widetilde z\|_{\ell^2}<\varepsilon$ for one of these finitely many lifts. Thus $J(B_V)$ is totally bounded with centers in itself. Its closure $C:=\overline{J(B_V)}$ is also totally bounded: a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for $J(B_V)$ is an $\varepsilon$-net for $C$ by the triangle inequality and the definition of closure. The set $C$ is complete because it is closed in the complete Hilbert space $H$: every Cauchy sequence in $C$ converges in $H$, and closedness keeps its limit in $C$. By [F4], $C$ is compact. The unit-ball criterion in [[def-compact-linear-operator]] now shows that $J$ is compact.

Each coordinate vector $e_j$ satisfies $a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(Je_j,Jv)_H$. For any nonzero $u\in V$, $\frac{a(u,u)}{\|Ju\|_H^2} =\frac{\sum_j\lambda_j|u_j|^2}{\sum_j|u_j|^2}\ge1,$ with equality exactly when $u_j=0$ for all $j\ge3$. Therefore the first eigenvalue is $1$, its full eigenspace is $E$, and the next eigenvalue is $3$.

The restriction of the continuous form to $V_h=E$ is the identity form, so both Ritz values are $1$ and the full cluster eigenspace is $E_h=E$. For every $u\in E$, $u\in V_h$, so the definition [F2] gives $\delta_a(E,V_h)=0$; likewise the gap from $E$ to $E_h$ is zero. The cluster theorem [F3] therefore applies with $r=1,s=2$ and its gap conclusion is attained exactly.

For each $h$, choose $u_h=e_1$ when $h$ is an even positive integer and $u_h=e_2$ when $h$ is odd. Both are unit Ritz eigenvectors for the same repeated eigenvalue $1$. Their successive energy distances are $\|e_1-e_2\|_a=\sqrt2$, so $(u_h)$ is not Cauchy and cannot converge. This does not contradict step 3.1: the invariant subspace remains exactly $E$, while the repeated eigenspace supplies no preferred basis vector.
